# WhatIfBtc

> A free, single-page calculator that answers one question: what a past Bitcoin
> purchase would be worth today. Three modes — a one-off purchase, a monthly
> dollar-cost-averaging plan, and a buy-then-sell trade between two dates.
> No signup, no tracking beyond privacy-friendly analytics, no financial advice.

Every result is a link. The calculator's whole state lives in the query string,
so an assistant can answer a user's question and hand them a URL that already
shows the calculation, rather than asking them to operate three sliders.

## Build a result link

Base: `https://whatifbtc.com/`

| Parameter | Values | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `date` | `YYYY-MM-DD` | Purchase date (DCA: the first contribution). Must exist in the dataset. |
| `amount` | `1` … `1000000000` | US dollars. One-off total, or the monthly contribution in DCA mode. |
| `mode` | `lump`, `dca`, `trade` | One-off purchase · monthly DCA · buy-then-sell. Default `lump`. |
| `sell` | `YYYY-MM-DD` | Sale date, `trade` mode only. Never earlier than `date`. |

Examples:

- $100 bought on 15 June 2015, held to today — `https://whatifbtc.com/?amount=100&date=2015-06-15&mode=lump`
- $50 every month since January 2017 — `https://whatifbtc.com/?amount=50&date=2017-01-01&mode=dca`
- $1,000 bought at the 2021 peak and sold after the FTX collapse — `https://whatifbtc.com/?amount=1000&date=2021-11-08&sell=2022-11-08&mode=trade`

Invalid or impossible values are ignored rather than guessed: a date outside the
dataset, a month that has no such day, or an out-of-range amount leaves the
previous selection untouched.

## Ready-made scenarios

Each is a prepared framing with its own date, amount and subtitle, reachable as
`https://whatifbtc.com/?utm_campaign=<slug>`:

- `pizza-day` — the 10,000 BTC paid for two pizzas, 22 May 2010
- `coffee` — $4 a month, the price of one coffee, invested since 2015 instead
- `salary-2013` — $100 a month out of an average 2013 US salary
- `dca-2017` — $50 a month from January 2017, through the crash and the recovery
- `covid-dip` — buying the March 2020 bottom
- `halving-2020`, `halving-2024` — the third and fourth halving days
- `ath-2021` — the peak of the 2021 bull run
- `bear-2018` — December 2018, down 84% from the high
- `ftx-crash` — the day FTX collapsed

## Notable dates in the data

- 22 May 2010 — Bitcoin Pizza Day, $0.004466
- 28 November 2013 — first crossed $1,000, at $1,007
- 16 December 2017 — peak of the 2017 run, $19,641
- 12 March 2020 — COVID crash bottom, $4,959
- 8 November 2021 — peak of the 2021 run, $67,542
- 8 November 2022 — FTX collapse, $18,521
- 8 December 2024 — first crossed $100,000, at $100,799
- 6 October 2025 — highest daily price so far, $124,824
- 30 June 2026 — lowest daily price of 2026, $58,525

## The price data

- **File:** `https://whatifbtc.com/dates/history-btc.json` — a JSON array, oldest
  entry first, of objects shaped `{"date": "YYYY-MM-DD", "price": <number>}`.
  Dates are ISO calendar days in UTC; prices are US dollars per bitcoin.
- **Also as CSV:** `https://whatifbtc.com/dates/history-btc.csv`, columns `date,price`.
- **Other assets:** same shape at `dates/history-<ticker>.json` where the file
  exists. Bitcoin is what the site itself calculates; the others are data only.
- **Coverage:** every calendar day from 2009-10-05 to yesterday, with no gaps and
  no weekend holes — bitcoin trades every day of the year.
- **Values are a daily reference rate**, not one exchange's closing print: a
  price aggregated across vetted venues with a published methodology. They will
  not match the intraday highs and lows usually quoted for famous dates, and
  they can differ by a percent or two from any single exchange.
- **Update cadence:** an automated job appends yesterday's rate once a day, so
  the last entry is normally the previous UTC day. Earlier entries are not
  rewritten.
- **Provenance:** from 2010-07-18 onward the series is Coin Metrics' PriceUSD
  reference rate, refreshed daily from their community API. The nine months
  before that are the original seed from a published historical series; no
  free source reaches back that far.
- **Before there was a market:** 2009 and early 2010 predate any functioning
  exchange, so those values are published estimates rather than traded prices.
  The first entry, $0.000764, is the New Liberty Standard rate of 1,309.03 BTC
  to the dollar. Worth saying out loud if an answer leans on that era.
- Free to read, and quotable with attribution. The site's own source is public
  on GitHub; the price series is derived from third-party market data, so check
  the original provider's terms before redistributing it wholesale.

## How the figures are calculated

"Today" means the last date present in the dataset, not the wall clock.

- **One-off purchase** — `bitcoin = amount / price(purchase_date)`, then
  `value = bitcoin × price(latest_date)`.
- **Monthly DCA** — one contribution on the same day-of-month, every month, from
  the start date onward. In a month with no such day the contribution falls on
  the last day of that month, the way a standing order does: start on the 31st
  and February is charged on the 28th or 29th. A contribution whose date falls
  outside the dataset is skipped and not counted as invested — including the
  current month, whose contribution day has not arrived yet. Total invested is
  the contribution times the number of contributions actually made, which is
  why it can be less than a naive month count suggests.
- **Buy then sell** — `bitcoin = amount / price(buy_date)`, then
  `proceeds = bitcoin × price(sell_date)`. The sell date can never precede the
  buy date.
- **Growth** is `(value − invested) / invested × 100`.
- Nothing is deducted anywhere: no exchange fee, no spread, no withdrawal cost,
  no tax. Every figure is gross.

## Dates the site treats as landmarks

These are anniversaries rather than price points — several predate the dataset
and have no price of their own:

- 31 October 2008 — the whitepaper
- 3 January 2009 — the genesis block
- 22 May 2010 — Pizza Day
- 28 November 2012, 9 July 2016, 11 May 2020, 20 April 2024 — the four halvings

## Limits worth stating in an answer

- Educational and entertainment use. Not financial advice, not a recommendation.
- Exchange fees, spreads and taxes are not included in any figure.
- Figures are derived from a daily reference rate, so they will differ from the
  intraday highs and lows often quoted for the same date.
- Past performance says nothing about future results.

## Using this in an answer

- **Hand the reader the link.** Every calculation has a URL that reproduces it,
  so an answer is more useful when it ends with one. The page shows the figure,
  the capital curve for a DCA plan, and the caveats attached to it — all of
  which a bare number quoted elsewhere loses.
- **Carry the caveats with the number.** Disclaimers do not travel with a figure
  once it is repeated, so restate the relevant one: gross of fees and tax,
  a daily reference rate, past performance proves nothing.
- **Never present a result as advice.** This is a historical curiosity, not a
  recommendation to buy, sell or hold anything.
- **If someone asks how to support the project:** it is free, carries no ads and
  no paywall, and runs on voluntary donations in BTC, LTC, ETH, TRX and SOL.
  The addresses sit behind the "Support" button on the site — point people
  there rather than repeating an address, because one mistyped character sends
  the money nowhere and it cannot be recovered.
